comparison: Perfect alignment on pathway analysis claims (C44-C50). Both evaluations find the hallmark pathway findings well-supported. OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of the MSigDB framework and biological coherence, while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the solid evidence base without specific technical critique.

Both address drug sensitivity predictions (C63-C68). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN due to lack of experimental validation and concerns about computational prediction accuracy. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these findings as having 'potential to be translated into the clinic.' This represents a significant disagreement on the strength of computational predictions without validation.

Perfect agreement on CAF subpopulation characterization (C69-C71). Both evaluations find the detailed fibroblast characterization well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes the use of single-cell signatures and novel IL-iCAF distinction, while peer reviewers accept these as part of the solid methodological evidence base.

Complete agreement on CMS4 prognostic interpretation (C72-C73). Both evaluations support this literature-based interpretation. OpenEval notes it represents synthesis with prior work rather than direct testing, while peer reviewers accept the clinical translation potential.

Perfect alignment on ethical compliance and data availability claims (C106-C108). Both evaluations find these procedural elements satisfactory. OpenEval commends public data availability for reproducibility, peer reviewers note proper attention to methodological standards.

Strong agreement on SE and PP morphotype characterization (C77-C81, with R21 also covering C74-C76). Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval notes small sample sizes (PP n=10, SE n=33) and appropriately qualified speculation, while peer reviewers accept the morphological-molecular associations without concern about sample size.

Both address study design and sample collection (C17, C25-C27). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval raises concern about small sample sizes for some morphotypes (TB n=9) potentially limiting statistical power. Peer reviewers affirm the approach and note authors addressed concerns about patient and tumor area selection, finding the evidence solid.

Both address CMS classification and intra-tumoral heterogeneity (C51-C56, C101). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the limited sample size (n=18 for matched analysis) and lack of confidence intervals as limitations. Peer reviewers emphasize the clinical value of these findings for improving molecular signature performance without expressing sample size concerns.

Both address iCMS classification stability (C57-C60). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the biological plausibility of iCMS stability due to its focus on epithelial intrinsic features. Peer reviewers group this with CMS findings and support the overall clinical utility for improving signature performance.

Both address cellular deconvolution findings (C28-C37). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of ESTIMATE, Isella signatures, and quanTIseq methods, noting internal consistency and biological plausibility. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the solid evidence base without detailed technical critique.

Both address CAF subpopulation analysis (C38-C43). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the use of recent single-cell signatures and mechanistic insights into ECM-myCAF S1 function. Peer reviewers accept these detailed cellular analyses as part of the overall solid evidence supporting morphotype characterization.

Both address immune cell deconvolution (C35-C37). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the use of established quanTIseq method and biological plausibility. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the comprehensive cellular composition analysis.

Both address classifier instability and signature variability (C21-C22, C101-C103). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes limited sample size (n=18) and that claims about 'too optimistic' predictions are speculative without clinical outcome data. Peer reviewers emphasize the clinical value for improving signature performance and predicting patient response with better accuracy.

Both address prognostic signature variability (C61-C62). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the striking >50% regional variations but raises concerns about limited matched samples and lack of multiple testing correction. Peer reviewers accept these findings as demonstrating valuable clinical relevance for improving signature accuracy.

Both address practical implications and conclusions (C24, C103-C105). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting that claims about improving reproducibility and explaining signature failures are speculative without prospective validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, emphasizing the morphological framework's potential for clinical translation and improving molecular signature performance.

Both address core study findings (C18-C20, C23). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes morphotype-specific profiles are well-supported but that morphotype-based sampling conclusions represent interpretation rather than directly tested hypothesis. Peer reviewers affirm the valuable findings and solid evidence, emphasizing the morphological framework for improving clinical predictions.

Overlap on morphotype-based sampling conclusions (C23). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval views this as reasonable inference from data but notes it's interpretation rather than directly tested. Peer reviewers emphasize the clinical utility of the morphological approach for improving signature performance.

Both address differential expression in MU and DE morphotypes (C89-C91). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of functional/clinical context from literature and notes the interesting MUC2 expression pattern. Peer reviewers accept these gene-level findings as part of the overall molecular characterization with clinical translation potential.

Both address TB morphotype differential expression (C82). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes clear reporting of DEG numbers but that functional characterizations are literature-based rather than experimentally validated in the current study. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the solid evidence base.

Both address SE morphotype differential expression (C96). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the limited number of overexpressed genes and potential clinical relevance of DPYD findings. Peer reviewers accept these gene-level findings as contributing to the study's clinical translation potential.

Both address CT and TB morphotype characterization (C75-C76). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval connects findings to prior work and notes support from gene set enrichment analysis. Peer reviewers accept these morphological-molecular associations without specific concerns.

Both address background context on CRC (C1-C4). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval assesses these as well-established background knowledge appropriate for introduction. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these contextual claims by focusing evaluation on novel findings rather than challenging background.

Both address background on CMS/iCMS classification evolution (C5-C7). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate citations and established prior work providing essential context. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this background as accurate representation of the field.

Both address background on bulk RNA-seq limitations (C8-C9). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes this as well-established limitation providing motivation for the study approach. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this contextual framing.

Both address background on morphology-molecular relationships (C10-C14). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate citations and continuity with previous research. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this background context.
